1:
Adam Clarke maps the sign first: the girdle left to rot was a type of the way the glory of the people would be marred through a long captivity, and the scene near the Euphrates named the land of their distress; he dates the discourse to the reign of Jeconiah. The first question is whether he went. Matthew Henry calls it an old dispute and inclines to the vision, since it seems hard to imagine him sent on two journeys that would each have taken a week when he could ill be spared at home. John Calvin agrees: the prophet did not actually go, but set the thing before the eyes of a deaf people by a lively description, what the rhetoricians call a scene presented to view. John Wesley gives the reason, that it was a very long journey from Anathoth to the river, and John Gill says simply that it was done in a vision. Charles Ellicott holds out against them all. The name used is the one everywhere else rendered Euphrates; the suggestions that it means a river generally, or that it stands for Ephratah with its caves in the rocky country towards the Dead Sea, rest on nothing but the assumed improbability of a double journey of two hundred and fifty miles, which he will not weigh seriously. He adds that the form of the name is nowhere found standing for Ephratah.

The command not to wet the girdle divides them further. Henry takes it practically, that the girdle was to be kept stronger and less likely to rot, since linen wastes almost as much with washing as with wearing. Clarke reads it the opposite way, that it was unwashed the better to represent the uncleanness of the people. Ellicott presses the priestly setting: the linen girdle was part of the prophet’s own priestly dress, so the people, figured as the girdle of Jehovah, appear chosen for consecrated uses; and since a priest washed often, the command was exceptional. The unwashed girdle stands for guilt unpurified by any contact with the clean water of repentance, and this, he says outright, is much more natural than an interpretation that begins from the idea that water would have spoilt the girdle and finds in the command a symbol of God’s care for his people. Calvin canvasses five explanations, among them a rabbinic view he judges inconsistent with the passage; the one he thinks most suitable is that nothing was to be done by the prophet to cause the rotting, so the decay might be seen to proceed from the people themselves.

Henry fills in the picture: it was worn for a name and a praise, probably a fine sash such as officers wear in the east, and the sight of it would be the stranger on a man who, like John Baptist, wore no soft clothing and probably used a leathern one; the hiding place was chosen so that when the river rose the girdle would be wet and when it fell would dry again, and would rot sooner than if always wet or always dry. Keil and Delitzsch read the burial in the cleft as a burying in the rocky soil of the river bank, and the many days as the seventy years of the captivity. Ellicott makes the same equation more cautiously, guessing at seventy days as a symbol of the seventy years, and would render the hiding place a cleft rather than a hole, since the lower course of the river runs through an alluvial plain so that a rocky valley points to its upper course. Calvin reads the hole as the figure of an ignoble condition, the people removed from the sight of men and from the common light of day, and the length of time as necessary, since in a short while the girdle would not have rotted.
8:
The sign is now explained, and its first word is disputed. John Calvin reports that other interpreters render it unanimously as pride, and that the versions give reproach, insolence and strength; but the noun can be taken two ways, and he has no doubt it means excellency, with only one authority agreeing. What is meant, on his reading, is the dignity with which God had favoured the seed of Abraham, and the two halves of the figure then harmonise: he had prepared them as a belt, and then cast them into a cavern to lie without light and without glory. He then takes from them the confidence by which they deceived themselves. They might have gloried in God, he allows, had they acted from the heart; but when they arrogated all things to themselves and deprived him of his authority, it was vanity to keep professing his name and saying they were his people, since he was no God to them and they had rejected his yoke. Charles Ellicott reaches the same sense from the object. The girdle was the part of the dress on which most ornamental work was lavished, a usual gift among princes, and therefore the natural symbol of the outward glory of a kingdom; and since Jeremiah was a priest, he thinks besides of the embroidered girdle of the priestly dress, made for glory and for beauty.

On the tenth verse Calvin fixes the cause of the calamity: the people had rejected the teaching of the prophets. This, he says, was far more grievous than falling away through ignorance, since men often go astray when the teaching of truth is taken from them; but when God shows the way and exhorts by his servants, it is an inexcusable hardness to repudiate such kindness. He notes that the verb to walk carries a road with it and an end in view, and that a contrast is understood: the people despised the way pointed out in the law and chose as if by design their own errors. The word for serving, he adds, covers worship and not obedience only. John Gill makes the refusal active: the prophets pressed them and importunately desired a hearing, and they would not give it. Ellicott corrects two renderings, preferring stubbornness to imagination and profitable for nothing to good for nothing, and notes that the same thought returns in the figure of the potter’s vessel, while a later chapter partly reverses it, the good figs there standing for the exiles who learnt repentance and the bad for those who stayed.

At the eleventh verse Ellicott observes that the parable takes in not Judah only but the other great division of the people, the sense of national unity being still strong in his mind: the whole collective Israel had been the girdle of Jehovah, consecrated to his service and designed to be to him what a girdle is to a man. Calvin uses the verse against a foolish confidence. They promised themselves perpetual happiness because God had chosen them, and it would have been a perpetual glory had they not violated their pledged faith; but their defection made the covenant void so far as they were concerned, though God never suffered his own faithfulness to fail. He concedes what they claimed and turns it back on them: they swelled only with wind, and their impiety was the less tolerable for its ingratitude, nothing being baser than that men so favoured should reject the bounty that honoured them. On the three nouns at the end he takes name for renown, praise for celebrity and glory for ornament, and holds them heaped for amplification; the election of God, he adds, was a bond of mutual union, that he might not be separated from his people. Gill notes only that the girdle in the figure is girt tight to the man.
12:
A second parable follows, and the commentators are chiefly interested in why it fell flat. Matthew Henry supposes the saying was already a common proverb, and that the people ridiculed the prophet for it, asking whether they did not know that every bottle would be filled with wine; he thinks they may have been touchy because they took it for a reflection on their drinking, and that in part it was so intended. To that he has the prophet answer that they shall have their bottles full, but not of such wine as they desire. Adam Clarke supplies a reason from the season: the vintage promised well, so the saying looked like a plain statement of what anyone could see, and they asked whether a revelation was needed for it. John Calvin puts the objection more fully: this was like saying a tankard is made to carry wine, a thing known to children and unworthy of a prophet. His answer is that God chose a trifling and as it were frivolous saying on purpose, to rouse a people asleep in their delusions and to show they could not see what was most evident: they all knew bottles were made for wine, but did not understand that they were the bottles.

Charles Ellicott traces the germ of the figure to the phrase drunken but not with wine, and to the thought that the wrath of God produces a confusion like that of drunkenness. He is precise about the vessel: not the skin commonly used for wine but the earthen jar, the potter’s vessel of another prophet. The prophet, he says, is bidden to proclaim a dark saying which in its literal sense would seem the idlest of truisms, and the people, not understanding that the wine was the wrath of God, repeat his words half in astonishment and half in mockery. Henry turns the figure round: those who by their sins have made themselves vessels of wrath shall be filled with it as a bottle is filled with wine; and a drunken man is fitly compared to a cask, since when the wine is in, the wit and the wisdom and the virtue are out. John Wesley names it the wine of astonishment, and Clarke spells out the mechanism: the wrath shows first in confounding their counsels, so that they fall out among themselves; he quotes the old adage that those whom God means to destroy he first makes foolish.

Ellicott notes that the kings sit for David as his successors, the plural pointing to the four caught in the sufferings that fell on Judah, and that the drunkenness is that of strong drink, probably palm wine. Calvin asks what the drunkenness is and offers two answers, that God would give them up to a reprobate mind or make them drunk with calamities, and judges from the context that the first is meant, since to deprive men of a right mind is to prepare them for vengeance. He dwells on the list of ranks: kings thought they should not be blended with the common people, the priests reckoned themselves sacred, the false prophets had a similar pride, but the prophet ties them all in one bundle. His lesson is that nothing on earth is so high that it need not submit when the glory of God and the authority of his truth are vindicated. On the dashing together Ellicott observes that the Hebrew idiom is a man against his brother, which carries a force the English lacks, pointing to what we should call the crash of a falling kingdom when all the bonds that hold society together are broken; John Gill reads the same clause of internal broils, men destroying one another instead of helping. Keil and Delitzsch add that the threat is coupled with an exhortation to give God the glory before judgment falls, by confessing apostasy and returning.
15:
John Calvin hears the doubled summons as evidence that the prophet was derided or ignored and had to defend his commission: in saying that the Lord has spoken he affirms that he brings nothing of his own, so that the people contend with him in vain, the contest being between them and God. He fixes on the clause forbidding pride as naming the root of the trouble, since the cause of their contumacy was that they dared to quarrel with God, the main principle of obedience being humility, when men acknowledge that they are nothing. Charles Ellicott refers the clause to the besetting sin already named, and adds a shrewd point about the two signs: the marred girdle and the broken jar are humiliating things in themselves, and were therefore a trial to a proud people. John Gill notes that the doubled summons marks the closest attention.

The command to give glory divides them sharply. Ellicott takes it as it stands where a man is abjured to confess a hidden theft, giving glory by confessing the truth even when the truth is a sin that involves punishment, and says this fits the context better than the general sense of ascribing praise: confess your guilt before it is too late for pardon. Keil and Delitzsch agree, making it an acknowledgement of the divine glory by confession of apostasy, and Gill, John Wesley and Adam Clarke all read it the same way, as confession of sin and submission before the judgments fall. Calvin alone refuses that sense here. He knows it is elsewhere used of confessing the truth, and cites the same abjuration; but here, he says, it is to ascribe to God what properly belongs to him and to acknowledge his power so as to be submissive to his word, since whoever denies faith to the prophets robs him of his glory.

The following clause is disputed on grammar. Calvin reports that all the versions render the verb intransitively, before it grows dark, but insists it must be causative, the form requiring it and the second clause naming God as the agent; he rejects the suggestion that the sun be supplied as subject, the sun not being said to send darkness by setting. Ellicott is exact about the mountains: the word is used only of the coolness and then the gathering gloom of evening, never of the dawn, so they are mountains of twilight, the deepening shadows being a vivid touch, the gloaming passing into the midnight of the shadow of death. Clarke reads it practically, taking the light they look for to be prosperity and the obstacles those they cannot surmount without light.

On the weeping Calvin finds the weight in what is left unsaid, that the prophet would cease to address them: nothing then remains but to hide in some corner and mourn, his office being at an end, so that the warning they now despise will itself be withdrawn. He observes that two feelings are joined in the prophet, a bold spirit in denouncing vengeance and at the same time commiseration; he might have wept for his own blood, but had regard above all to the favour of God. Clarke says the same briefly: if they will not hearken there is no remedy, and nothing is left him but to go in secret and mourn. Ellicott dwells on the tenderness of the words as characteristic of the prophet, comparing the tears shed over the city and the heaviness of Paul, and finds a parallel to the secret places in the withdrawal of our Lord to a solitary place: nothing remained for one whose labours were fruitless but silent sorrow and intercession. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the phrase as the concealment to which mourners love to withdraw that they may weep the more freely, and note that the carrying away of the flock is stated as already past.
18:
Three questions open here, and the first is who is addressed. Charles Ellicott settles the second title: the word is not the usual feminine of king but means the great lady, the style of a queen-mother, used elsewhere of the mother of Asa and here probably of Nehushta. John Calvin agrees that the lady is the mother and not the wife, since she was her son’s associate in the kingdom, though he attaches the prophecy to a different reign. Adam Clarke names Jeconiah and his mother, under whose tutelage he was left as a boy king; John Gill reports that reading as the general one but prefers a later king and his wife, since the captivity threatened here is complete and the earlier was not. Ellicott is exact about the crowns: the word rendered principalities means head-tires, the diadems of kingly state, and occurring nowhere else it may have been coined by the prophet or drawn from the court vocabulary.

Calvin makes the address to the throne into a rule for teachers. God intended, he says, to rouse the whole community by showing that he would spare neither king nor queen; hence the truth the prophets announce stands above all the greatness of the world. Kings think themselves not only exempt by privilege from every law but free from any obligation to modesty, and from that elevation despise God and his prophets; whereas God gave the prophets his word that they might shut their eyes to the splendour of the world and pull down every height. He concludes that no one chosen to teach can discharge the office faithfully unless he dares to reprove kings and queens, since the word of God is not restricted to the common people but subjects all to itself. Matthew Henry puts it briefly, that their sorrows would be great indeed, and that if they ask why these things come, the answer is their obstinacy in sin. Keil and Delitzsch summarise the section as the fall of the kingdom and the captivity of Judah, with upbraidings against the city for her idolatry, and render the opening as a command to sit low down, the crown of their glory falling from their heads.

The cities of the south divide them further. Ellicott takes the phrase as a fixed term for a district south of the capital, and reads the clause strategically: the plan of the invader, as of an earlier one, was to blockade the cities of that region so that they could send no assistance, and then to attack the city itself; both verbs, he adds, should be present. Gill agrees that the cities of Judah in the south are meant, shut up when besieged or so destroyed that none could go in or out, and reports the alternative of Egypt only to reject it. Calvin adopts that alternative against almost all interpreters. He takes the cities to be those of Egypt, since the people looked there for refuge whenever they were attacked, so that the prophet declares the gates of their expected asylum closed with none to open them; he argues that he would have spoken more plainly had he meant Judah, and that in Jerusalem such a way of speaking would have been ambiguous, especially as the enemy is placed in the north a verse later. Clarke keeps to the geography without the dispute: not the cities of the north only but those of the south too would suffer, since the invader would go from one extremity of the land to the other; John Wesley notes simply that the cities of Judah lay southward from the country of the invaders. On the closing words Calvin declines the received rendering and offers a literal one of his own, the transmigration of Judah entire, the transmigration of retributions, observing that the last word is never used adverbially and is plural only once elsewhere.
20:
John Gill notes that the two opening verbs are written in the singular and read in the plural, so the summons may be addressed to the king or to the people, the Greek supplying the name of the city. Charles Ellicott explains the irregularity as deliberate, the feminine singular verb with a masculine plural pronoun combining the personification of the city with the multitude of her inhabitants; the beautiful flock of the other towns had been committed to her care, and she must give account of her stewardship. Gill takes the flock for the people entrusted to the king as sheep to a shepherd; Adam Clarke asks plainly where the multitudes of men, women and children now are, and John Wesley answers that in the multitude of the people is the honour of the king. John Calvin hears the two empires set against each other: whenever the invaders from the north are named, the people turn their eyes to Egypt, and the prophet bids them look further and see enemies coming from another quarter. The question about the flock he attributes to pity, the prophet having seen by the Spirit the whole land deserted, and being the only one with eyes to see.

The twenty-first verse is the hardest here. Ellicott says it requires an entire retranslation and gives one: what wilt thou say, for he shall set over thee as head those whom thou taughtest to be thy familiar friends. This was the end of the alliance in which the kingdom had trusted; and he offers a second construction, in which those set over her are those whose supremacy she had acknowledged in order to court their alliance. Calvin reaches a similar sense from the history: they had called in one empire against another and so accustomed foreigners to rule, setting them in effect over their own heads, which is why it is no wonder they are now grievous to them. He notes a change of number, common in the prophets, the singular pointing to the head of the army and the plural to the whole force, and applies the clause to the invaders, not, as some do, to God. Clarke fixes the moment historically: ever since one king submitted to Assyria the kings of Judah never regained independence, and their enemies were taught to be their masters. Wesley adds that they will have nothing to say but be wholly confounded, and Calvin makes the silence the point: they are talkative now, but when the enemy distresses them it will not be the time for their loquacity.

Matthew Henry takes the question of the twenty-second verse as coming from either of two hearts. It may be a sinner quarrelling with God and refusing correction, who could not see that he had done anything to provoke him and in his heart charged God with unrighteousness; or a sinner returning, for if there comes but a penitent thought God takes notice of it and is ready by his Spirit to impress the conviction. Calvin makes the point sharper: hypocrites do not merely claim righteousness before the world but deceive themselves; and had they sinned once, or in one kind, there would have been some hope of pardon, but an uninterrupted course of sinning left no room for sparing them. On the figure he observes that clothes serve two ends, protection from cold and decency, and that the prophets speak of uncovering when they mean exposure to public reproach. Ellicott identifies the skirts as the flowing train worn by women of rank, whose removal was the sign of extremest degradation, and would render the next clause outraged, made to walk barefoot like a slave. Clarke reads it of a defenceless state known everywhere; Wesley traces the phrases to the practice of soldiers stripping prisoners; and Henry adds the sequel, that they made their pride appear and God will make their shame appear.
23:
The comparison here raises three questions, the first being who is meant. John Gill lists the candidates: the word is the Cushite, rendered Ethiopian by the Greek and Latin, taken by one version for an Arabian people nearer Judea, and by the Targum and Syriac for the Indian. John Calvin reports the same division, that many learned men deny the Ethiopian is meant though all the early versions but one so render it; he notes that the text does not call the skin black but marks it as of a colour different from that of the Jews. Charles Ellicott supplies the local background instead: invasions from the south and the traffic with the upper valley of the Nile had made such figures familiar objects.

The second question is how far the impossibility reaches, and here Adam Clarke and Calvin both pull back. Clarke says the expression does not imply that the thing is as impossible in a moral sense as in a natural one, but only that it is extremely difficult and not often to be expected; and what is impossible to man, he adds, is still possible to God. Calvin goes further and refuses the verse to his own side of a contemporary argument. Learned men of his age, he says, are unwise to cite it as proof that there is no free will in man, for what is spoken of is not simply the nature of man but a habit contracted by long practice; even a philosopher who strongly defended free choice, he notes, admitted that it is not in a man’s power to do right once he is so immersed in his vices as to have lost it. The doctrine they want, he grants, is true and confirmed elsewhere, but this text does not carry it, since the prophet is not speaking of what a man is from the womb but condemning a people hardened by long habit. Keil and Delitzsch state the harder view without qualification, that wickedness had so grown to be the nature of Judah that it could as little cease from it as either trait could be altered.

On the scattering the voices agree in substance and differ on the wind. Ellicott is precise about the figure: the English word means the stalks the reaper leaves standing, but the Hebrew is used of the broken straw left on the threshing floor, which the first gale carries off; the wind he identifies as the burning wind of the Arabian desert, and Keil and Delitzsch as the strong east wind. Calvin instead calls it the wind of the south, the most violent and pestilential in that country, and declines the suggestion that Egypt is alluded to, seeing no reason to seek a refined explanation for a common form of speech. Clarke calls it a tempestuous wind proverbially severe, and Gill notes that they could no more resist the enemy than stubble the wind. Calvin adds the contrast that gives the figure its edge: they boasted that they were trees planted in that land by the hand of God, but wanted the living root of piety and so were to be driven off like straw. At the last verse Ellicott takes the doubtful word for the upper garment or lap of the dress, and would render the closing clause in a lie, the worship of gods that were no gods; Keil and Delitzsch report the argument that the word can only mean garment and never measure, and answer that this is no conclusive proof, since both senses come from one root. Calvin hears the verse as stripping away a boast: they had said the land was theirs by hereditary right and God their heritage, both true in their place, but another lot is now measured out to them; Clarke names the falsehood they trusted as idols and lying prophets.
26:
John Calvin hears the sentence as a retaliation exactly matched to the offence. The particle at the head of the verse marks something mutual, as though God said he too would have his turn and repay their ingratitude in kind: as they had despised him, so he would expose them to reproach. What made the offence so shameful was that they had put the Egyptians and their idols in the place of God, and could have done him no greater dishonour than by transferring his glory to their own figments. He works over the wording, noting that the verb means to strip off so as to lay bare and that the threat is to turn the skirts up over the face; the versions all differ, and one, which has the uncovering done before rather than over, he says imparts no meaning at all. The phrase, he says, means the uncovering of the uncomely parts, as when a woman is condemned to be stripped and set before the public, and it carries its force because God had taken the character of a husband to his people. John Gill gives the same sense and fixes the fulfilment at the burning of the city and the temple, and John Wesley reduces it to a line. Charles Ellicott notes only that the threat repeats the one made a few verses earlier and that its wording is identical with a passage in another prophet.

Adam Clarke alone stops to question the human practice behind the image. It was the custom, he says, to punish lewd women by stripping them and exposing them to public view, or by throwing their clothes over their heads as the verse describes; and he breaks off to ask whether this was the way to correct the evil. The doubt is his own, and none of the others raise it.

At the last verse the voices agree that the adulteries are figurative. Calvin observes that the sins of the people were various, and that the prophet elsewhere charges them with drunkenness and plunder as well, but that here he speaks only of their false worship, so that the adulteries are idolatries and not the whoredom which nevertheless prevailed among them. Gill says the same, that the word is not to be taken literally, though they were greatly guilty of that sin too, and Wesley glosses it in two words. On the second image Calvin is blunt: the comparison to the neighing of animals is far more shameful than if the prophet had said their lusts, since it makes them not merely inflamed as adulterers are but driven like beasts, and sets out the furious ardour with which they followed their own inventions. He adds that the word rendered lewdness properly means thought, and that the prophet used it to strip off a colour with which the people painted themselves: they claimed to intend the worship of God while heaping up rites the law never prescribed, and were inwardly full of unchastity, like a woman who thinks of nothing but her lovers.

Clarke uses the closing question to reopen the argument he had begun four verses earlier. From the fact that the question is asked at all, he argues, we see that the thing was difficult but not impossible; it was only their obstinate refusal of the grace of God that made it impossible. A man cannot change himself, he grants, but he may pray to God to do it and come to him through Christ, and the power to pray and believe is still at hand: if he will not use it, he must perish. It is the sharpest statement in the chapter of the difference between difficulty and impossibility, and leaves a door open at the end of the sentence.
